n: In this lesson we consider the question of identifying victims in disasters. The aim of the work is to find the remains, identify them and establish the cause of death. The lesson has five sections. The first section is devoted to concepts and management: DVI, stages and mandate. The second section is about the scene: recognising, recording and collecting remains. The third section includes triage in the mortuary and detailed examination. In the fourth section identification is studied, that is, criteria, DNA and confirmation. The fifth section is devoted to complex cases, work with the family, a terrorist attack and a practical case.

t: Section 1: DVI and management in brief
n: The first section is devoted to DVI and management. DVI means comparing the data from before death, that is, AM, with the data from after death, that is, PM. Let us go through the questions in the table one by one. A disaster is a loss that exceeds the capacity of society. The source of the procedure is the INTERPOL DVI guide. Decision-making belongs to the local legal authority. The basic rule is that at least one primary criterion is needed for identification. And finally, the answer to the question of what takes priority: first quality, then speed.

t: Disaster and the need for identification
n: What is a disaster and why is identification necessary? The threshold of a disaster is set by jurisdiction, from 2 to 10. A disaster is damage exceeding the capacity of society, and may be natural: storm, tsunami, fire. Disasters caused by humans include aviation accidents and terrorist attacks. Identification is needed for several reasons. First, it is a mark of respect for the deceased. Second, it is necessary for relatives. Third, legally: questions of inheritance and remarriage are settled. Fourth, it is also needed for the criminal case.

Disasters are divided into open and closed. In the closed type there is a list of victims, for example in an air crash. When the list is complete, the process ends, because everyone is accounted for. In the open type, the number of victims is unknown. An example is a building explosion. In such a case a definition of the "identifiable" part is needed, and resources are also taken into account. That is, in a closed disaster the condition for finishing is clear, whereas in an open disaster it must first be determined which part will be identified.

t: INTERPOL: the five stages of DVI
n: According to INTERPOL, DVI has five stages. The first stage is the scene. The second stage is the mortuary, where PM data are obtained. In the third stage AM data are gathered. The fourth stage is comparison. The fifth stage is the debrief, that is, the final discussion. Remember: these stages cover the whole process from the disaster to burial.

t: AM and PM data: the pair to be compared
n: Now on AM and PM data. They form a pair to be compared. AM data, that is, before death, include dental records, X-rays and casts. A fingerprint is taken from an object or workplace. DNA may be taken from an object or a relative. PM data, that is, after death, include the dental state, a fingerprint if preserved, a DNA sample and personal effects. AM data are gathered as early as possible. Matching is done manually or by software.

t: The multidisciplinary team: who does what
n: In identification work, specialists work not alone but as a team. Let us see who does what. The pathologist evaluates the cause of death and the large parts. The odontologist compares dental records. The anthropologist deals with skeletal remains and the biological profile. The radiologist carries out analysis of X-rays and PMCT, that is, postmortem computed tomography. The fingerprint and DNA specialist compares the print and the DNA profile. This multidisciplinary team works because the task of each specialist is clearly delimited.

t: Questions to be settled from the start
n: Before starting work, a number of questions must be settled. These decisions are entered in the preparation plan. First question: who advises and who is responsible. Second: which specialist is needed on site, an anthropologist or an archaeologist. Third: what is the scope of the examination, full or only identification. Fourth: the identification mandate, that is, which part counts as "identifiable". Fifth: contact with the family and media, where the information must be unified and consistent.

t: The event determines the scope of examination
n: The event determines the scope of examination. If the cause is known, the examination may be shortened. Let us look at the examples in the table. In the WTC event, 2001, no autopsy was done. In the American Airlines 587 case, autopsy was mandatory by law. In the Malaysia Airlines 17 event, autopsy was done only on selected persons. In the Victoria fire case, 2009, if there was suspicion of another cause, this was referred to the coroner. Thus the scope is determined each time by the event itself.

In terminology, one word may take on two meanings. An imprecise term leads to a wrong conclusion. Therefore a clear definition is needed: what a complete body is, what a body part is, what a fragment or piece is. The Christchurch event, 2019, is an example. In medicine "fragmentation" denotes the state of preservation of the remains. In the police, however, this word means ballistic evidence. That is, the same word has a different meaning for different specialists.

The second section is devoted to the scene. Wrong collection complicates work in the mortuary. Let us look at the table. The first condition is recognising the remains. Then come mapping and recording of the location. A specialist is needed for fragmented or burnt remains. The consequence of error is commingling and repeat searching.

At the scene, three actions are performed in sequence: recognise the remains, record their location, then collect and package. Unrecognised remains are not recorded or collected. Therefore the first step is to recognise them. The preliminary assessment determines the subsequent stages. That is, the assessment made at the scene sets the direction of all the work that follows.

Collection without a specialist increases time and cost. Let us look at the examples in the table. In the WTC event, 2001, the remains were collected by firefighters, with the result that additional commingling occurred. In the Victoria case, 2009, the search was done without an anthropologist, so sites had to be searched again. In the MH17 event, 2014, the remains were collected by local volunteers, with the result that identification slowed.

t: Mapping method by type of site
n: A map of the distribution of remains is needed for the investigation and the inquest. The mapping method is chosen according to the type of site. On a large open area, drones and laser scanners are used. For destroyed or buried remains, the total station and photogrammetry are suitable. For small buried fragments a grid is used, and recording is done manually or by GPS. In low-technology conditions the INTERPOL grid and a printed label are used.

Why does location matter for burnt remains? Heat changes volume, colour and shape. Burnt fragments are brittle and scattered. The process is as follows: strong heat acts, as a result of calcination the bone becomes white and brittle, and a DNA profile is not obtained. Therefore the location must be recorded, which later allows the fragments to be refitted.

Quality control is carried out at the scene. The form for fragmented remains is under review at INTERPOL. Unacceptable actions: placing several persons in one bag and attempting to reconstruct the body on site. The recommended actions are as follows: involve a specialist in the initial collection, check the form without sealing the bag, and check the correctness of the location sketch.

t: A specialist is needed even with few victims
n: A specialist is needed even when there are few victims. Here it is not the number but the state of the remains that decides. Let us consider two examples. In the Rue Erlanger event, 2019, the number of victims was 10, and the result of the specialist's work became visible when commingling was prevented. In the Wales fire case, 2017, the number of victims was 6, and the victims were in a separate room.

The third section is devoted to the mortuary. The rule is that all remains are examined, regardless of size. Let us look at the table. The aim of triage is to separate what is not human and to set priority. Detailed examination is carried out for identification. The DNA sample is taken as early as possible. Storage is done at −80 °C or by drying.

In triage the order and participants are clear. First, complete bodies and large parts are examined. Then fragments are examined. The examination is carried out by the pathologist and anthropologist. The work is done with imaging and physical examination. Remember: the inside of the bag is also photographed.

Examination of fragments proceeds step by step. First we separate what is not human. Then we separate duplicate bones. Then we join fragments that match at the fracture. On each fragment the fingerprint and teeth are checked first. At the slightest suspicion of commingling, the fragments are separated. Documentation is by photography and chain of custody.

What should be recorded in detailed examination? The INTERPOL form is complex for fragments. The primary identifier is a fingerprint or teeth, which allows identification without DNA. Individual features, that is, anomalies and surgical marks, help identification. Perimortem injury is needed to reconstruct the mechanism of the event. The description of each fragment helps to detect commingling or a wrong number.

Work can be carried out in parallel in the mortuary. Such examination allows the sample to be obtained sooner. That is, if work proceeds in several directions at once, waiting for sampling is shortened.

t: X-ray and PMCT: how they help
n: How do X-ray and PMCT help? First, the contents of the bag can be seen, and the position is recorded "in situ". Second, there is the possibility of refitting parts and finding fragments of one person. Third, individual features are detected: filling, implant, healed fracture. Fourth, comparison with AM can be approximate, for example by sinuses and vascular grooves. It must be remembered: in a 3D model the accuracy of the metric method is unknown.

t: Biological profile: which features are useful
n: The biological profile gives a preliminary "picture" until AM data are found. For this, population-specific standards are required. The most useful features are sex and age at death. Features of limited use are race, that is, ancestry, and stature. Skeletal diseases and anatomical variants are given as additional features.

There are main questions on skeletal remains. Burnt bone is examined only by a specialist. Is it human? On a whole bone this is easy, on a fragment a specialist is needed. Does it belong to one person? For example, if two skulls or two left femora are found, it is not one person. How are sex and age determined? Sex from the skull and pelvis, age by group. Stature is approximate, determined from tables. For the question of who the person is, reliable AM data are needed.

The fourth section is devoted to identification. Measurement alone does not identify; matching identifies. The primary criteria are fingerprint, DNA, teeth and a unique medical feature. For fragments the main method is DNA. The rule of confirmation is that there must be at least one primary criterion.

The criteria fall into three groups. Primary criteria: fingerprint, DNA, teeth and a unique medical feature. Secondary criteria: deformity, mark and scar, X-ray, personal item, special clothing. Supportive criteria: clothing, photograph, place, and gait analysis from camera. A unique feature or a combination of features increases the weight.

Why is odontology the first choice? First, it is a quick and inexpensive method. Second, its strong point is resistance to putrefaction and fire. In comparison, the AM record is compared with the PM state. Making a chart alone is not enough; the records must match. The odontologist makes a chart even if there is no AM. The difficulties are connected with soft tissue, rigor and burning.

In choosing a sample for DNA there are the following assessments. In soft tissue the risk of contamination is high. Therefore soft tissue is not recommended on a small fragment. Bone is preferred, and its spongy part is better. A tooth is a good source, but the method is complex. The condition for a tooth is that odontological analysis is done first.

t: Avoiding contamination of the DNA sample
n: The DNA sample must not be contaminated. For a reusable scalpel, 10 % bleach is used. Investigators also give an elimination sample. Rules by material: on soft tissue, after the outer layer, a new scalpel is taken. On whole bone a disposable scalpel is used. On sawn bone the blade is cleaned or replaced. The sample size must be sufficient for retaking.

t: The definition of "body part" is not uniform
n: The definition of "body part" is not uniform. The definition is announced at the start of the event. Variants are given in the table. First variant: human tissue larger than 5×5 cm. Second: tissue with bone of at least 5 cm. Third: tissue "with a chance of being identified". Fourth: anatomically identifiable, with no size. In the MH17 case, uncalcined bone of >3–4 g was used.

In the Bayesian approach, the strength of evidence is assessed. A feature need not be unique. Let us consider the terms. Prior odds is the probability before applying the method. Likelihood ratio, that is, LR, shows the strength of the evidence: it is the ratio of two hypotheses. Posterior odds is the prior multiplied by the LR. A low LR together with others may be strong evidence.

The path to confirming identification is as follows. First, AM and PM are compared. Then confirmation by a secondary feature. Then a body diagram is made, in which duplicate parts are checked. Finally, a board is held and handover takes place. The rule: at least one primary criterion is required.

The fifth section is devoted to complex cases. Every disaster is unique, so the response is adapted. Cases and main difficulties: the problem of injured persons with unknown names among the survivors. In a terrorist attack, work proceeds together with the criminal investigation. In migrant deaths there is no AM list. In contact with the family, fragments are identified at different times.

Identification of survivors is done in four groups. Identifying the living shortens the list of the missing. In Paris, 2015 and Nice, 2016 this proved effective. The first and second groups are those uninjured or conscious, in which the role of the anthropologist is minimal. The third and fourth groups are unconscious patients, who are identified by DNA swab, fingerprint and teeth. In the medical centre, personal data are passed to the team.

t: Terrorist attack: criminal investigation and DVI
n: In a terrorist attack, the criminal investigation and DVI are conducted together. In the Paris event, 2015, there were ~90 fragments, and identification lasted ~6 months. In the criminal investigation the priority task is to find the perpetrator and prevent a new attack. The DVI team, however, is part of the investigation, separates victim and perpetrator, and is subject to the law of the country.

Migrant deaths require a different approach. This case is regarded as an international, long-lasting disaster. The difficulties and consequences are as follows. There is no list of the missing, so there are no AM data. Data are in different states, so cooperation is necessary. DNA, teeth and fingerprints are as a rule absent, so an anthropological profile is needed.

The scale and lessons of the 2004 tsunami. Dead 226,000+, affected states 13. In Thailand 5,395 victims were found. Those identified mainly by teeth, ≈3,308. Identification lasted 3.5 years. Those identified were citizens of 40 states. The lesson is that if the dead are properly stored, identification later becomes easier.

There are principles of contact with the family. The family can change its decision at any time. Issues and recommendations: identification may not be achieved, and the family is told in advance. Fragments are identified at different times, and the family chooses the method of notification. The level of information may be a full file, without photographs, or a diagram. If the perpetrator's remains are commingled, separation is not always possible.

t: Family and showing to the court: Shoreham
n: The question of showing to the family and court is considered through the example of Shoreham. The form of images in court is agreed in advance. Rejected variant: 3D reconstruction based on PMCT, because it is too graphic. Variants used: a body diagram for completeness, a table with scientific and plain terms, and in court line drawings, which is the example of Wales.

We consider the experience of major events in the table. The number of victims and the number of fragments do not match. WTC, 2001: ~22,000 fragments, 1,637/2,749 identified (2019). AA587, 2001: 2,100 fragments, all identified in 28 days. MH17, 2014: 8,000+ DNA samples, DNA from 296/298 victims. Shoreham, 2015: 1,200+ body parts, all identified, examination ~6 weeks. Paris, 2015: 129 parts and a complete body, all identified in 1 week.

t: Number of victims and fragments found
n: The number of victims and the number of fragments found do not correspond to each other. Even a small number of victims may yield many fragments.

Now let us consider a training case. This is a conditional training case, not real work. Given: explosion of a residential building, number of victims unknown, remains burnt and fragmented. Questions: is the disaster open or closed? Which specialist is needed on site? Can DNA be obtained from white, brittle bone? Which sample is preferable?

The answer to the case consists of applying the principles. The type of disaster is open, since the number of victims is unknown. An anthropologist or archaeologist is needed on site. A DNA profile is not obtained from calcined bone. As a sample, bone is preferred, not soft tissue on a small fragment. The location of the fragment must be recorded, which allows refitting. The rule: record the location and store separately.

Summary of the lesson. Quality control stands above speed. The plan: mandate, scope and terms are determined in advance. At the scene a specialist prevents commingling. In the mortuary, triage is done first, then detailed examination. For identification at least one primary criterion is needed. With the family, work honestly and consistently and offer ready options.

The review questions correspond to the content of the sections. First question: list the stages of DVI. Second: what is the difference between an open and a closed disaster? Third: why is the location of burnt skeletal remains recorded? Fourth: which criteria are among the primary? Fifth: what options are there in contact with the family?
